clinicalPearls: A benign osteochondrosis of the ischiopubic synchondrosis in children
It represents exuberant or asymmetric ossification at the junction of the ischium and pubis during normal development
It may be asymptomatic or cause groin, buttock or hip pain and a limp
The key issue is that its radiographic appearance can mimic osteomyelitis, Ewing sarcoma or a healing fracture
MRI can show marrow oedema that adds to the confusion with more serious pathology
Recognition of this normal variant avoids unnecessary biopsy and treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Van Neck disease reflects a normal but sometimes asymmetric or prominent stage in the ossification and fusion of the ischiopubic synchondrosis, the cartilaginous junction between the ischium and pubis that normally fuses in later childhood. The expanded, sometimes fragmented, appearance and associated marrow oedema are part of physiological development, but they can radiographically resemble infection or tumour. It is essentially a self-resolving developmental variant rather than a disease.
additionalDifferentials: Ewing sarcoma or other bone tumour
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs, ideally with comparison of both sides and follow-up
MRI where infection or tumour must be excluded
Inflammatory markers to help exclude infection
Clinical correlation and observation over time
Avoidance of biopsy once the diagnosis is recognised
redFlags: Systemic features or raised inflammatory markers suggesting infection
Aggressive imaging features or a soft-tissue mass suggesting tumour
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and resolves as the synchondrosis fuses, with an excellent prognosis once more serious mimics are excluded.
pitfalls: Mistaking the normal variant for osteomyelitis or Ewing sarcoma and performing biopsy
Failing to compare with the contralateral side
Not correlating imaging with the benign clinical picture
management: Recognition as a benign, self-limiting developmental variant to avoid unnecessary intervention
Reassurance and observation, as the condition resolves once the ischiopubic synchondrosis fuses
Activity modification with simple analgesia such as paracetamol or NSAIDs for pain and limp
Comparison radiographs of both sides with follow-up imaging to confirm the diagnosis
Inflammatory markers and MRI reserved for cases where osteomyelitis or tumour must be excluded
Avoidance of biopsy once the diagnosis is recognised
